The [[number]] '''4,294,967,295''' is a whole number equal to 2{{sup|32}}&nbsp;−&nbsp;1. It is a [[perfect totient number]], meaning it is equal to the sum of its iterated [[totient]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Loomis|first1=Paul|last2=Plytage|first2=Michael|last3=Polhill|first3=John|title=Summing up the Euler φ Function|date=2008|journal=College Mathematics Journal|volume=39|issue=1|pages=34–42|doi=10.1080/07468342.2008.11922272|jstor=27646564|s2cid=44013467}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Iannucci, Douglas E. |author2=Deng, Moujie |author3=Cohen, Graeme L. | title = On perfect totient numbers | journal = [[Journal of Integer Sequences]] | volume = 6 | year = 2003 | issue = 4 | pages = 03.4.5 |bibcode=2003JIntS...6...45I |mr=2051959 | url = http://www.emis.de/journals/JIS/VOL6/Cohen2/cohen50.pdf}}</ref> It follows 4,294,967,294 and precedes 4,294,967,296. It has a factorization of <math>3 \cdot 5 \cdot 17 \cdot 257 \cdot 65537</math>, which are the first five [[Fermat number|Fermat primes]].

In computing, '''4,294,967,295''' is the highest [[Unsigned int|unsigned]] (that is, not negative) [[32-bit computing|32-bit]] integer, which makes it the highest possible number a 32-bit system can store in a word sized [[Processor register|register]].

== In geometry ==
Since the prime factors of 2{{sup|32}}&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 are exactly the five known [[Fermat prime]]s, this number is the largest known odd value ''n'' for which a [[regular polygon|regular]] [[n-gon|''n''-sided polygon]] is [[constructible polygon|constructible using compass and straightedge]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Lines|first1=Malcolm E|title=A Number for your Thoughts: Facts and Speculations About Numbers from Euclid to the latest Computers...|date=1986|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=9780852744956|page=[https://archive.org/details/numberforyourtho0000line/page/17 17]|edition=2|url=https://archive.org/details/numberforyourtho0000line/page/17}}</ref><ref name="OEIS">{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A004729 |name=Divisors of 2^32 - 1 (for a(1) to a(31), the 31 regular polygons with an odd number of sides constructible with ruler and compass)}}</ref> Equivalently, it is the largest known odd number ''n'' for which the angle <math>2\pi/n</math> can be constructed, or for which <math>\cos(2\pi/n)</math> can be expressed in terms of [[square root]]s.

Not only is 4,294,967,295 the largest known odd number of sides of a constructible polygon, but since constructibility is related to factorization, the list of odd numbers ''n'' for which an ''n''-sided polygon is constructible begins with the list of factors of 4,294,967,295. If there are no more Fermat primes, then the two lists are identical. Namely (assuming 65537 is the largest Fermat prime), an odd-sided polygon is constructible if and only if it has 3, 5, 15, 17, 51, 85, 255, 257, 771, 1285, 3855, 4369, 13107, 21845, 65535, 65537, 196611, 327685, 983055, 1114129, 3342387, 5570645, 16711935, 16843009, 50529027, 84215045, 252645135, 286331153, 858993459, 1431655765, or 4294967295 sides.<ref name="OEIS"/> If there are more numbers in this list, they must be at least 2{{sup|2{{sup|33}}}}+1 (approximately 10{{sup|2585827973}}), because every intervening Fermat number is known to be composite.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/FermatNumber.html|title=Fermat Number|publisher=Wolfram MathWorld}}</ref>

== In computing ==

The number 4,294,967,295, equivalent to the [[hexadecimal]] value {{base|FFFFFFFF|16}}, is the maximum value for a [[32-bit]] [[integer (computer science)|unsigned integer]] in [[computing]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Simpson|first1=Alan|title=Alan Simpson's Windows XP bible|date=2005|publisher=J. Wiley|location=Indianapolis, Indiana|isbn=9780764588969|page=999|edition=2nd|chapter=58: Editing the Windows Registry}}</ref> It is therefore the maximum value for a [[variable (computer science)|variable]] declared as a 32-bit unsigned integer (usually indicated by the {{code|unsigned}} codeword). The presence of the value may reflect an error, overflow condition, or missing value.

This value is also the largest [[computer memory|memory]] address for CPUs using a 32-bit address bus.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Spector |first1=Lincoln |title=Why can't 32-bit Windows access 4GB of RAM? |url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/2013751/why-cant-32-bit-windows-access-4gb-of-ram.html |website=PC World |publisher=IDG Consumer & SMB |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307031902/http://www.pcworld.com/article/2013751/why-cant-32-bit-windows-access-4gb-of-ram.html |archive-date=7 March 2016 |date=19 November 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref> Being an odd value, its appearance may reflect an erroneous (misaligned) memory [[pointer (computer programming)|address]]. Such a value may also be used as a [[magic debug values|sentinel value]] to initialize newly allocated memory for debugging purposes.

Internet Protocol version 4 ([[IPv4]]) uses a 32-[[bit]] addresses which limits the [[address space]] to {{gaps|4|294|967|296}} (2<sup>32</sup>) unique addresses.

In 2004, 800 aircraft over Los Angeles were put in danger when the LA Air Route Traffic Control Center lost radio contact with all of the aircraft for about three hours, delaying 400 flights and cancelling 600, due to a computer design that kept time by starting at 4,294,967,295 milliseconds and counting down to zero, or 49 days, 17 hours, 2 minutes and 47.295 seconds. Some people were aware that the system needed to be restarted at least every 30 days, but the root problem was the choice of such a small number.<ref>{{cite book|last=Parker|first=Matt|title=Humble Pi: A Comedy of Maths Errors|chapter=Chapter One: Losing Track of Time|publisher=Penguin Random House UK}}</ref>

On May 4, 2021, [[Nasdaq]] temporarily suspended price feeds for [[Berkshire Hathaway]] [[Class A share]]s ({{NASDAQ|BRK.A}}), which reached $421,000. Nasdaq stores stock prices as 32-bit unsigned integers in increments of ten-thousandths of a [[United States dollar|dollar]], so the maximum price that could be represented was $429,496.7295.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Osipovich |first1=Alexander |title=Berkshire Hathaway's Stock Price Is Too Much for Computers |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/berkshire-hathaways-stock-price-is-too-much-for-computers-11620168548 |access-date=6 May 2021 |work=The Wall Street Journal |date=4 May 2021}}</ref>
